rv.q: This lavishly mounted stage adaptation of the beloved 1964. Disney film proves that sometimes more really can be more, delivering a family-friendly spectacle that should enchant children and adults alike.
Her clipped diction, clasped hands and stiff poise make it clear this Mary is nobody's servant.
Disney's Mary Poppins is a handsome, well-crafted family musical that delivers the goods without quite achieving greatness.
Even young children with great patience (is that an oxymoron?) may grow restless with the implicit lecturing between those moments when Mary flies, literally and figuratively.
It's spectacular, and not even slightly boring, but anyone familiar with Walt Disney's 1964 film version of "Mary Poppins" is likely to come away asking what happened to the charm.
Every element of the evening blends with an animated vivaciousness that lifts your spirits as easily as Mary Poppins takes off in flight, sailing to the upper balcony at the end of the evening.
Tap shoes fly vigorously in the show stopping "Step In Time" routine, highlighted by a Gavin Lee bit that is sure to be one of the most memorable moments of the season.
Mary Poppins is a show that succeeds despite itself, offering enough theatrical magic to make you believe that a spoonful of sugar really can help the medicine go down.
This adaptation teeters between saccharine and tart in what feels like a creative tug-of-war.

cn.t: A lavish spectacle with dazzling effects and theatrical magic, but critics are divided on its emotional coldness and tonal inconsistency. The production enchants with stagecraft while struggling to balance saccharine sentiment and darker elements.
